passage:
Dear Hafsa Appi,
Board results came out on Wednesday. It's Sunday and I still haven't looked. The link is sitting in my messages. Ammi thinks I'm being cool about it. I'm not.
Every time I pick up the phone my stomach drops, so I put it down and go play cricket in the lane. For about an hour I forget. Then at night I lie there doing sums: if maths went badly, if I don't get science stream, if everyone asks.
The worst part is that Karim sir said the re-evaluation forms close on Tuesday, and I don't even know if I need one.
Can you call me tomorrow evening? If you're on the phone, I think I can open it.
Your little brother,
Noor

qa.q: When did the board results come out?
qa.a: Board results came out on Wednesday.

qa.q: What is Noor feeling each time he picks up the phone?
qa.a: His stomach drops with dread about a bad score; putting the phone down gives an hour of relief, but at night the worry comes back bigger.

qa.q: Is Noor's plan to open the result with Hafsa on the phone a good one?
qa.a: Yes; a calm person on the line makes it easier to look, and knowing by Monday leaves time to decide about the re-evaluation form before Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel tender and a little worried 🤍, glad Noor asked for help and eager to call so he isn't facing it alone.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy avoiding his exam results to put off the sting, while not knowing makes him more anxious and less prepared.

Okay Pradeep, since you asked. Me, Siddharth, the guy who hid a sealed envelope for nine days. The school sent our report cards home sealed, and I just knew physics had gone badly. So I put the envelope under my cricket kit in the cupboard and didn't touch it.
Every day it sat there I felt worse. I couldn't eat properly, I kept checking whether Mummy had cleaned the cupboard. I'd tell myself, tomorrow, I'll open it tomorrow.
Then the class group chat said physics remedial classes had started, and the signed report card was due. Mummy saw that before I did. When we finally opened it, physics was bad, yes, but not the disaster I'd been imagining. And I had already missed three remedial classes. That's the part that really hurt.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth hide the report card envelope?
qa.a: Siddharth put the envelope under the cricket kit in the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep promising to open it tomorrow?
qa.a: Not looking put off the sting of a bad physics mark, so each delay felt like a small relief, even though the worry grew every day.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: By hiding the result Siddharth missed three remedial classes; opening it on day one, maybe with Mummy, would make the bad news smaller and leave time to act.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy to learn about the report card from the class group chat?
qa.a: Mummy may feel hurt and worried at finding out from other parents, and sorry that Siddharth carried the fear alone for nine days.

grounding: It shows a teenager postponing the sting of a report card, which only leaves the teenager more anxious and less prepared.

passage:
I'm Sangeeta, Tushar's didi, and I watched this whole thing from the next room. The unit test marks went up on the school portal on Monday. His classmate Gopika messaged him, "Marks are up!!" Tushar turned his phone face down.
All week he said he'd check later. He was jumpy at dinner, snapped at Amma about nothing, and stayed up late watching videos. I can't say for sure what was going on inside him, but he looked like someone carrying something heavy.
On Friday I sat on his bed and said, "Want to look together? Whatever it is, it's just one test." He was quiet for a long time, then handed me the phone. Chemistry was low. He exhaled, like it was almost a relief to finally know.

qa.q: Who told Tushar the marks were up?
qa.a: His classmate Gopika messaged him, "Marks are up!!"

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling during the week he didn't check?
qa.a: He was probably anxious about a bad mark and dreading the sting; being jumpy, snapping at Amma and staying up late suggest the not-knowing weighed on him more than the mark itself.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help Tushar face the result?
qa.a: Sangeeta offered to look together and made it smaller by saying it was just one test, so Tushar could hand over the phone without feeling judged.

qa.q: How is Amma affected by Tushar's week of avoiding the marks?
qa.a: She gets snapped at for nothing, taking the edge of a worry she doesn't even know about.

grounding: It shows, through an older sister's eyes, a teenage boy avoiding his test marks to delay the sting while the not-knowing makes him more anxious.

passage:
Tuesday: The class group buzzed at four: "Half-yearly results on the school app!" Yash, fourteen, put his phone in the drawer and went to play football till dark. At dinner his mother, Rashmi, asked, "Results?" "Not out yet," he said, and his stomach turned.
Friday: At maths tuition, Sir began going over the half-yearly paper. Everyone else had checked their marks and brought questions. Yash hadn't looked. He sat with his notebook closed, heart thumping, not following a word.
Sunday: Rashmi found him awake at one in the morning. He finally opened the app with her beside him. Maths was bad: 41. Science was fine. "Okay," Rashmi said. "Now we know what to fix." Yash let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

qa.q: Where did Yash put his phone when the results came out?
qa.a: He put his phone in the drawer.

qa.q: Why might not checking the app have felt better to Yash on Tuesday?
qa.a: Avoiding the marks postponed the sting of a bad result, so for a few hours he could pretend nothing had changed.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Opening the app on Sunday with his mother beside him; once he knew maths was the problem he could start fixing it, and the fear shrank 🙂

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt finding Yash awake at one?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and tender, realising the results had been weighing on him for days.

grounding: A teenage boy avoids checking his results to put off the sting, and the not-knowing leaves him more anxious and lost in class.

passage: Sahil, you've been hiding that report card envelope under your pillow since Friday. Your Mola Dolma knows everything. Let me tell you about my brother Pasang. In Darjeeling, when we were young, results were pinned on the school gate. Pasang was fifteen. The day they went up, he took the long road home, round the tea garden, so he wouldn't pass the gate. For two weeks he wouldn't let anyone say the word "results". He barely slept, and he snapped at our mother. Then the teacher came to our house. Pasang had failed one subject, and the re-test was in four days. Four days, when he could have had two weeks. He passed, just. But he always said the waiting was worse than the marks. So. Shall we open it together, over tea?

qa.q: Why did Pasang take the long road home round the tea garden?
qa.a: So he wouldn't pass the gate where the results were pinned.

qa.q: Why do you think Pasang wouldn't let anyone say the word "results"?
qa.a: Hearing it brought the dread closer, so blocking it out gave him a little relief, even though he barely slept.

qa.q: What choice does Dolma offer Sahil, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To open the envelope together over tea, so Sahil faces the news early and with company, leaving time to act instead of losing days to fear.

qa.q: What might those two weeks have been like for Pasang's mother?
qa.a: She had to live with his snapping and sleepless nights without knowing why, which was likely worrying and hurtful.

grounding: An elder recalls a brother avoiding his results, which left him anxious and with less time to prepare for a re-test.

Class teacher's note, 20 May.
The half-yearly results went up on the school portal on Friday. By Monday, Ojas still hadn't looked. Tejas told me Ojas kept changing the subject whenever marks came up and had stopped eating lunch. When I called Ojas aside, he said, "If I don't see it, it's not real yet." He looked exhausted. I asked whether not knowing had made the weekend better. He shook his head; he had barely slept. So I sat with him in the staffroom and we opened it together. Maths was low, forty-four. Everything else was fine. His shoulders dropped. "That's it?" We made a plan for maths on the spot, and I let his parents know about the plan, not just the mark.

qa.q: What did Ojas score in maths?
qa.a: Ojas scored forty-four in maths.

qa.q: Why did Ojas avoid checking the results?
qa.a: Ojas felt afraid of bad news, and not looking seemed to keep the sting away, even though it left him anxious and unable to sleep.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why did it work?
qa.a: The teacher opened the results with Ojas and made a maths plan straight away, turning a vague dread into one clear problem with a next step.

qa.q: What had the weekend been like for Tejas, watching Ojas?
qa.a: Tejas was probably worried, noticing Ojas changing the subject and skipping lunch, and chose to tell the teacher.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding his results to postpone the sting, and feeling more anxious for not knowing.

passage:
Friday, 11 p.m.
The board results came out at noon. The message has been sitting on my phone for eleven hours. I haven't opened it. Every time I pick up the phone I put it down again. As long as I don't look, maybe I passed maths. Maybe I didn't. Both are true right now.
Tanuja messaged: "86!! What did u get??" I sent a heart and nothing else.
The weird thing is, not looking hasn't made me feel better. I've felt sick all day. I couldn't eat Biji's parathas. I keep inventing worse and worse numbers in my head.
Okay. Writing this so I'm brave. I'll open it with Biji sitting next to me. Right now.
Later: Maths 58. Not great. Not the disaster I'd imagined for eleven hours.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What did Tanuja score?
qa.a: Tanuja got 86.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel during those eleven hours of not looking?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt sick and anxious all day, inventing worse numbers, so not looking brought no relief at all.

qa.q: What finally helped Gurpreet open the result?
qa.a: Writing in the diary to feel brave and opening the result with Biji sitting alongside, so the news didn't have to be faced alone.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt getting only a heart back?
qa.a: Tanuja might have felt puzzled or worried, sensing something was wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding a board result to postpone the sting and becoming more anxious for not knowing.

The class ten results were out at noon, and everyone in the small town was crowding at the cyber cafe near the bus stand. Baljeet walked past it twice.

His friend Darshan waved from inside. "Come! I'll check yours!"

"Later," Baljeet called, and kept walking to the fields.

He sat under the neem tree till evening, pulling grass. Every time a motorbike passed, he wondered if someone was bringing the news. His stomach ached.

At home, his mother asked, "Did you see?" He shook his head.

The supplementary form deadline was in two days. Darshan finally came over with a printout. Baljeet had failed maths by a few marks. "If you'd checked this morning," Darshan said gently, "we could've gone to Sir today."

qa.q: When were the class ten results out?
qa.a: The results were out at noon.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet walk past the cafe and sit under the neem tree?
qa.a: He wanted to put off the sting of bad news, but not knowing left him anxious, with his stomach aching all afternoon.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do now, and what might help him next time?
qa.a: Now he can go to Sir with Darshan about the supplementary form; next time, checking with a friend beside him could make it easier to face.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel bringing the printout?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt worried for his friend and a bit frustrated that a day had been lost.

grounding: A teenager avoids checking results to delay the sting, but not knowing leaves him anxious and short of time.

The email from Ivan's school in Tallinn arrived on Friday: "Your term report is now available." Ivan archived it without opening it.

All weekend he helped his sister Rosa build a shelf, played football, and avoided his laptop. But at dinner he barely ate, and he woke at three in the morning thinking about chemistry.

On Monday his teacher mentioned a make-up test for anyone who had failed. "The list was in the report," she said. "The sign-up closed Sunday."

Ivan felt sick. That evening he opened the report with Rosa next to him. He had failed chemistry, but only just. Rosa helped him write to the teacher asking about another chance. He hit send, then sat back, tired but less tangled up.

qa.q: When did the make-up test sign-up close?
qa.a: The sign-up closed Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Ivan archive the email without opening it?
qa.a: He was afraid of bad news and wanted to delay the pain, even though avoiding it kept him anxious and awake.

qa.q: What helped Ivan finally deal with his results?
qa.a: Opening the report with Rosa beside him and writing to the teacher together made it easier to face.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ivan had opened the report on Friday?
qa.a: He could have signed up for the make-up test in time and avoided a weekend of worry.

grounding: A teenager avoids looking at his report to postpone the sting, and not knowing leaves him anxious and unprepared.

At the boys' hostel, the warden posted the mid-term marks on the notice board outside the dining hall. Ramesh took the long way round to dinner for three days so he wouldn't pass it.

His roommate Gurleen noticed. "You haven't looked, have you?"

"I'll look after the weekend."

"The tutor's extra classes start Monday. Names are on the list if you're below forty."

Ramesh shrugged, but he lay awake that night, imagining every subject had gone badly.

On Sunday Gurleen walked him to the board. Ramesh had passed everything except physics. His name was on the extra class list. He let out a long breath. "I thought it was all of them."

"Not knowing made it bigger," Gurleen said.

qa.q: Where did the warden post the mid-term marks?
qa.a: On the notice board outside the dining hall.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh take the long way to dinner for three days?
qa.a: He was scared of seeing bad marks and wanted to delay the sting, though avoiding them left him more anxious.

qa.q: What small step helped Ramesh face the marks?
qa.a: Gurleen walked him to the board, so he didn't have to look alone.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Ramesh's avoidance?
qa.a: Gurleen seems concerned and patient, seeing that not knowing was making Ramesh's worry bigger than the marks.

grounding: A teenager avoids checking marks to postpone the sting, but not knowing makes him more anxious.

passage:
Reena, you asked about my worst school habit. I'm Anand, and in Class 9 I didn't open my report card for eleven days.
It came in a sealed envelope. I knew maths was bad. So I put the envelope in my cupboard, under my cricket pads, and just didn't. Every time I thought of it, I felt a cold drop in my stomach, and I'd go out and play instead. For a few minutes that felt like relief.
But the relief never lasted. I kept dreaming about red ink. And there was a note inside the envelope: remedial maths classes starting that Monday, sign up by Saturday. By the time I opened it, I'd missed the first week.
My father wasn't even angry about the marks. He was sad I hadn't told him. He said, "We could have fixed this on day one." That line stayed with me. Bad news is smaller when it's early.

qa.q: How many days did Anand leave the report card unopened?
qa.a: Anand didn't open the report card for eleven days.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep the envelope under the cricket pads?
qa.a: Anand felt a cold dread about maths, so avoiding the envelope gave a few minutes of relief, though the relief never lasted.

qa.q: What did the father's line teach, and how can it be used?
qa.a: 'We could have fixed this on day one' shows that opening bad news early leaves time to act, like joining remedial classes on time.

qa.q: How did Anand's father feel about the eleven days?
qa.a: The father was sad rather than angry, wishing Anand had told him so they could fix it early.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoided opening a report card to postpone the sting, and missed the chance to prepare.

Monday. The mock entrance test scores went live at noon. Tejas's friends compared numbers in the canteen. Tejas said, "I'll check later," and put his phone in his bag. He felt lighter for an hour.
Wednesday. Anirban asked, "So? What did you get?" "Haven't looked." "Bro, it's been two days." That night Tejas couldn't sleep. He imagined a score of zero, of ten, the whole class laughing.
Sunday. Anirban came over and sat on the bed. "Log in. I'm right here."
Tejas logged in with shaking fingers. 112 out of 300. Not great. But not zero. The weak section was clearly physics.
"That's fixable," Anirban said. "Physics revision classes start tomorrow. You'd have missed them."
Tejas let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

qa.q: What score did Tejas get?
qa.a: Tejas got 112 out of 300.

qa.q: Why couldn't Tejas sleep on Wednesday?
qa.a: Tejas felt anxious and full of dread, imagining terrible scores, because not knowing let the fear grow bigger than the real number.

qa.q: What helped Tejas finally face the score?
qa.a: Anirban sitting with Tejas while logging in, which made the news shareable and showed physics was the part to fix.

qa.q: How does Anirban see the score?
qa.a: Anirban sees it as fixable and is glad Tejas looked in time for the physics revision classes.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids checking a test score to postpone the sting, becoming more anxious until a friend helps him look.

"Darshan, put the phone down a minute. You haven't opened your results link, have you? Your Gautam Mama knows that face.
When I was fifteen, the half-yearly marks were pinned on the school notice board just before Diwali. Everyone ran to see. I didn't. I told myself I'd look after the holidays, and I went off to burst crackers as if nothing was wrong.

After the holidays I finally looked. Maths: only just passed. If I had looked that first day, I'd have had three weeks of the maths teacher's extra classes. Instead the finals came and I was still behind.
